definition: The continuous production of all blood cell lineages from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.
A hormone made mainly by the kidney that stimulates red cell production; hypoxia increases its release.
The normal adult hemoglobin, a tetramer of two alpha and two beta chains that carries oxygen.
The sigmoid curve relating oxygen saturation to partial pressure; it shifts right with higher temperature, acidity, or 2,3-BPG.
A red cell metabolite that lowers hemoglobin oxygen affinity; stored blood loses it, shifting the curve left.
The body iron storage protein; serum ferritin reflects stores and falls early in iron deficiency.
The main plasma iron transport protein; its measured capacity rises in iron deficiency.
A plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin; low levels indicate hemolysis.
The bone marrow ratio of granulocyte precursors to erythroid precursors, normally about 3:1 to 4:1 in adults.
Blood cell production outside the marrow, such as in the liver or spleen, when marrow demand or space is exceeded.
Variation in red cell size, graded on the film and measured objectively as the RDW.
Variation in red cell shape seen on the blood film.
Red cells smaller than normal (low MCV), typical of iron deficiency and thalassemia.
Red cells larger than normal (high MCV), seen in B12 or folate deficiency and liver disease.
Reduced hemoglobin content in red cells, judged by widened central pallor on the film.
The pale center of a normal red cell, about one third of its diameter; wider pallor means hypochromia.
The last near-mature stage of red cell production, retaining residual RNA that stains as a network.
A small dense round red cell without central pallor, seen in hereditary spherocytosis and warm AIHA.
A fragmented red cell caused by mechanical damage, seen in microangiopathic hemolysis such as TTP.
Inherited underproduction of alpha or beta globin chains causing microcytic anemia with target cells.
An increase in immature neutrophil precursors such as bands and metamyelocytes in the blood, usually from infection.
An extreme benign leukocytosis above 50,000 cells that mimics leukemia but responds as a mature cell reaction.
Nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes on the film, suggesting marrow infiltration or stress.
The most immature precursor of a blood cell lineage; blasts above 20 percent define acute leukemia.
An azurophilic needle-like cytoplasmic inclusion in myeloblasts, classic in acute myeloid leukemia.
Coarse dark cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils seen with infection or inflammation.
A pale blue cytoplasmic patch in neutrophils, a remnant of rough endoplasmic reticulum seen with toxic changes.
A large lymphocyte with abundant cytoplasm responding to antigenic stimulation, common in viral infection.
A crushed or degenerated leukocyte without definite structure, common in films with many neutrophils.
A group of clonal marrow disorders with ineffective production, dysplastic morphology, and cytopenias.
A platelet count below the reference range; risk is judged by the count and any bleeding.
A platelet count above the reference range, either reactive or clonal as in essential thrombocythemia.
Platelets aggregating in an EDTA sample, which can falsely lower the automated count.
Platelets rosetted around neutrophils in EDTA tubes, a spurious in-vitro phenomenon.
The average platelet size reported by analyzers; larger values suggest young platelets or artifacts.
A falsely low platelet count caused by EDTA-dependent clumping, checked with a citrate sample.
A very large platelet, usually young and reactive, seen when production is increased such as in ITP.
Immune destruction of platelets causing isolated thrombocytopenia with giant platelets on the film.
An inherited absence of the GPIb receptor that prevents platelet adhesion, with giant platelets and bleeding.
An inherited absence of the GPIIb/IIIa complex that prevents platelet aggregation despite normal counts.
The additive in lavender-top tubes that binds calcium to prevent clotting for blood counts.
The required venipuncture tube sequence that prevents additive cross-contamination between tubes.
A specimen with ruptured red cells that releases hemoglobin, disturbing many analyte measurements.
Spinning a capillary tube to measure packed red cell volume; trapped plasma can raise the reading.
The distance red cells fall in an upright tube over one hour, raised by inflammation.
Coin-stack arrangements of red cells caused by reduced surface charge in protein-rich plasma.
The share or number of reticulocytes among red cells, reported as a percent or an absolute value.
A white cell count adjusted when nucleated red cells are counted by automated counters as leukocytes.
A ruled glass counting chamber of known depth used for manual cell counts.
The thin even area of a blood smear where the differential count is performed.
The vascular phase: vasoconstriction, platelet adhesion, and aggregation forming the platelet plug.
The coagulation cascade phase that converts fibrinogen to fibrin to stabilize the platelet plug.
A test of the extrinsic and common pathways, prolonged by factor VII deficiency or warfarin therapy.
A standardized PT ratio that uses the international sensitivity index of the thromboplastin reagent.
A test of the intrinsic and common pathways, prolonged in factor VIII, IX, or XI deficiency and heparin therapy.
The soluble plasma precursor of fibrin, measured by clotting time and low in consumption or dysfibrinogenemia.
A fibrin degradation product that rises when cross-linked fibrin is broken down by fibrinolysis.
Patient plasma mixed with normal plasma: correction suggests a factor deficiency, non-correction suggests an inhibitor.
The mediator that links platelets to subendothelial collagen during platelet adhesion.
The blood-to-citrate ratio in blue-top coagulation tubes; an incorrect fill alters results.
A chart of daily control values plotted around the mean with two and three standard deviation warning lines.
A combined set of single and multi-control decision rules used to accept or reject an analytical run.
A warning triggered when one control value falls outside two standard deviations from the mean.
A rejection rule when a single control value falls outside three standard deviations from the mean.
Two consecutive controls from the same level beyond two standard deviations on the same side, a systematic error.
Two control values in one run differing by more than four standard deviations, a random error.
Scattered control results on both sides of the mean, usually from pipetting or instrument noise.
Control results consistently on one side of the mean, usually from calibration or reagent bias.
A sudden sustained change in control values, suggesting a new reagent lot or calibration change.
A steady progressive drift of control values in one direction over several consecutive runs.
Reagent that bridges human IgG or complement on red cells, producing visible agglutination in direct and indirect antiglobulin tests.
Test of patient red cells for antibody or complement already attached in vivo; used in immune hemolysis, transfusion reaction and HDFN investigations.
Rare phenotype lacking H, A and B antigens on red cells. Anti-H in the plasma makes ordinary group O red cells incompatible.
Reduced serologic reactivity with anti-D. RHD genotyping distinguishes variants safely managed as D-positive, including weak D types 1, 2 and 3.
Passive anti-D used to prevent RhD alloimmunization in an unsensitized RhD-negative patient after exposure to RhD-positive fetal red cells.
Acid-elution stain that counts HbF-containing fetal cells among adult red cells to estimate fetomaternal hemorrhage and help determine the RhIG dose.
Decline of a previously detected red cell alloantibody below the assay detection limit; it may return with an anamnestic response after re-exposure.
Stronger alloantibody reactions with red cells homozygous for an antigen than with heterozygous cells, as seen with Kidd antibodies.
Acute hypoxemic, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema during or within 6 hours of transfusion, often associated with donor anti-leukocyte antibodies.
Cold-insoluble fraction of plasma rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII and von Willebrand factor; used mainly to replace fibrinogen.
Cylindrical structure formed in the renal tubules from a Tamm-Horsfall protein matrix that may trap cells, granules, lipid or crystals; casts show that a sediment finding arose in the kidney.
Glycoprotein that forms the matrix of urinary casts. Hyaline casts consist of it alone and increase with strenuous exercise, dehydration and fever.
Renal tubular cell or macrophage filled with absorbed lipid droplets; a sign of lipiduria in nephrotic syndrome. Cholesterol droplets inside show Maltese crosses under polarized light.
Dense, brownish granular cast formed from degenerating renal tubular epithelium; highly specific for acute tubular necrosis.
Urine fixed at the osmolality of plasma (specific gravity about 1.010) because the tubules can no longer concentrate or dilute the filtrate; typical of advanced chronic kidney disease.
Plasma glucose level, about 180 mg/dL on average, above which proximal tubular reabsorption by SGLT2 and SGLT1 is saturated and glucose appears in the urine.
Yellow, orange or pink color of centrifuged CSF supernatant from pigments of lysed red cells (oxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, bilirubin); supports subarachnoid hemorrhage over a traumatic tap.
Rules that classify a pleural effusion as an exudate if fluid/serum protein >0.5, fluid/serum LD >0.6, or fluid LD >2/3 of the serum upper reference limit; one criterion is enough.
Serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin. A gradient ≥1.1 g/dL indicates a high-gradient (transudative) effusion from portal hypertension; <1.1 g/dL suggests other, exudative causes.
Needle-shaped synovial fluid crystal of gout, strongly negatively birefringent: yellow when aligned with the slow ray of a red compensator, often inside leukocytes.
Calculated difference between measured cations and anions, Na − (Cl + HCO3). An increased gap signals unmeasured anions such as lactate or ketones in metabolic acidosis.
Measured minus calculated serum osmolality (2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8). An increased gap suggests unmeasured osmoles such as ethylene glycol or methanol.
Estimate of LDL cholesterol in mg/dL: total cholesterol − HDL cholesterol − triglycerides/5. Regarded as invalid when triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL.
Hemoglobin with glucose attached, reflecting average glucose over the red cell life span (about 2–3 months). Falsely low when red cell survival is shortened, as in hemolytic anemia.
Bilirubin conjugated with glucuronic acid in hepatocytes, making it water-soluble, and secreted into bile. A mainly unconjugated increase points instead to hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome.
Colorimetric creatinine method in which creatinine reacts with alkaline picrate. Bilirubin and other substances can interfere with the kinetic Jaffe method.
Ratio of AST to ALT activity. AST usually exceeds ALT in alcoholic hepatitis, whereas ALT usually exceeds AST in acute viral hepatitis.
Falsely low sodium on an indirect ion-selective electrode when excess lipid or protein reduces the plasma water fraction (electrolyte exclusion effect). A direct ISE gives the true value.
Lowest drug concentration in a dosing interval, collected just before the next dose is due. Used in therapeutic drug monitoring of drugs such as vancomycin.
Total calcium adjusted for low albumin, commonly by the Payne formula: total Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin in g/dL). Ionized calcium measures the active fraction directly.
Autoantibody against nuclear antigens. Screened by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells and reported as a titer and pattern; a high titer supports SLE and related connective tissue diseases.
Antibody to citrullinated peptides. Its sensitivity for rheumatoid arthritis is similar to rheumatoid factor's, but it is more specific, so the two are often tested together.

Autoantibody, most often IgM, directed against the Fc region of IgG. Supports a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, but it also occurs in other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections and healthy people.
Terminal complement complex that forms pores in target membranes and lyses cells. Deficiency of C5–C9 predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
Set of closely linked HLA genes on chromosome 6 inherited together from one parent. Each person has two haplotypes, so close relatives are the most likely HLA matches.
Pretransplant test in which recipient serum is incubated with donor lymphocytes and rabbit complement. Cell lysis shows donor-specific HLA antibodies (a positive crossmatch).

Syphilis algorithm that starts with an automated treponemal immunoassay and follows a reactive result with a quantitative RPR. Discordant results go to a second, different treponemal test such as TP-PA.
Supplemental test in the CDC HIV algorithm, run after a reactive antigen/antibody screen. It confirms antibodies and distinguishes HIV-1 from HIV-2; if it is negative, HIV-1 RNA testing follows.
IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen. It indicates recent (under 6 months) HBV infection and separates acute from chronic infection when HBsAg is positive.
Cell-mediated reaction caused by T cells and macrophages, with no antibody involved, that develops over 2 or more days. Examples are contact dermatitis and a positive tuberculin skin test.
A skin commensal organism isolated from only one of two or more blood culture sets collected within 24 hours, indicating a false-positive result introduced during collection.
Presumptive identification test for group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), used on beta-hemolytic colonies after enrichment-broth subculture to blood agar.
Double-disk diffusion test that detects inducible clindamycin resistance in erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible isolates; D-zone-positive isolates are presumed clindamycin resistant.
Staphylococcal gene encoding PBP2a, an altered penicillin-binding protein with low beta-lactam affinity that causes methicillin (oxacillin) resistance, as in MRSA.
Selective and differential stool medium on which E. coli O157 STEC forms colorless colonies because it does not ferment sorbitol within 24 hours.
In vitro immunodiffusion (immunoprecipitation) test that confirms diphtheria toxin production by Corynebacterium diphtheriae isolates.
Vaginal Gram stain score based on lactobacilli, Gardnerella/Bacteroides morphotypes and curved gram-negative rods: 0–3 normal, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 bacterial vaginosis.
Vaginal epithelial cell studded with adherent bacteria; one of the Amsel criteria for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis.
Blood film in which RBCs are lysed so parasites are concentrated; used to screen for malaria and other blood parasites, with the thin smear used for species identification.
Test such as PCR or antigen detection that identifies a pathogen without growing it; a positive result is followed by reflex culture to obtain an isolate for susceptibility testing.

OSHA term for body fluids treated like blood, including semen, vaginal secretions, CSF, synovial, pleural, pericardial, peritoneal and amniotic fluids, and any body fluid visibly contaminated with blood.
Written OSHA-required plan identifying jobs with occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens and the controls used; it is reviewed and updated at least annually.
Controls that isolate or remove the bloodborne pathogen hazard from the workplace, such as sharps disposal containers, self-sheathing needles and needleless systems.

OSHA term for liquid or semi-liquid blood or OPIM, items that would release blood if compressed, items caked with dried blood that can release it, contaminated sharps, and pathological or microbiological wastes.
Chemical hazard document in a standard 16-section format (for example, Section 8 lists exposure controls and PPE); SDSs must be readily accessible to employees during each work shift.
Word on a hazard communication label showing relative hazard severity: "Danger" for more severe hazards and "Warning" for less severe hazards.

Written program required by the OSHA Laboratory Standard (29 CFR 1910.1450) setting procedures, equipment, PPE and work practices that protect laboratory workers from hazardous chemicals; reviewed at least annually.
One of four containment levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) defining laboratory practices, safety equipment and facility construction; each level builds on the one below it.
Ventilated cabinet designed to provide personnel, product and environmental protection when appropriate practices are followed; used for procedures that can create infectious aerosols or splashes.
Shipping designation for low- or moderate-risk infectious specimens, triple-packaged in a leakproof primary receptacle, leakproof secondary receptacle and rigid or strong outer packaging.
